lesson.title: Decimals to Hundredths: Cents Make Sense!

steps.say: Let's start at the corner store in your neighbourhood. You hand the cashier a loonie — one whole dollar — and you get one quarter back as change. A quarter is twenty-five cents. But how much of a dollar is that? A dollar is a hundred cents, so a quarter is twenty-five out of one hundred. We write that as zero point two five dollars. That's what decimals are for — they let us name a piece of a whole thing.

visual.caption: One dollar = 100 cents. A quarter shades 25 of them.

steps.say: Here's the big idea. Take one whole thing — one dollar, one metre, one chocolate bar — and cut it into one hundred equal pieces. Each tiny piece is called one hundredth. One hundredth is written as zero point zero one. See that one little square? That is one penny out of a whole dollar. Small, but it still counts!

visual.caption: One whole cut into 100 equal squares. Just one square is shaded.

steps.say: Now, sometimes we cut the whole into only ten equal pieces instead of a hundred. Each of those bigger pieces is called one tenth, and we write it as zero point one. Look at the bar — one strip out of ten is shaded. And here's a neat secret: one tenth is exactly the same amount as ten hundredths. Ten pennies make one dime!

visual.caption: One whole split into 10 equal strips — one strip is one tenth, or 0.1

steps.say: So every digit after the dot has its own special seat. The first seat after the dot is the tenths seat, and the second seat is the hundredths seat. Let's read one dollar and thirty-five cents. The one sits in the ones seat, the three sits in the tenths seat, and the five sits in the hundredths seat. We say it out loud as one and thirty-five hundredths.

visual.caption: Ones, then tenths, then hundredths — each digit has its own seat

steps.say: Let's try our first example together. You have seven dimes in your pocket. Each dime is ten cents, so seven dimes is seventy cents. As a fraction of a dollar, that's seventy out of one hundred, which we write as zero point seven zero. And because seven dimes is also seven of the ten strips, it's seven tenths — zero point seven. Same amount, two ways to say it. Zero point seven and zero point seven zero are twins!

visual.caption: 7 dimes = 70 cents = 70 hundredths of a dollar

steps.say: Ready for one that's a little trickier? In art class you have two pieces of ribbon. One is zero point four metres long and the other is zero point three five metres long. Which one is longer? Careful — zero point three five has more digits, but that does not mean it's bigger! Let's put both on a number line and see.

visual.caption: Both ribbons marked between 0 and 1 metre

steps.say: Here's the trick that makes it easy. Change zero point four into hundredths by adding a zero on the end — zero point four is the same as zero point four zero, which is forty hundredths. Now compare forty hundredths with thirty-five hundredths. Forty is bigger than thirty-five, so the zero point four metre ribbon is longer — by five hundredths of a metre, which is five centimetres. Look at the picture: the blue squares are the thirty-five, and the extra squares are the five more.

visual.caption: 35 hundredths, plus 5 more hundredths, makes 40 hundredths

steps.say: So here's what to remember, my friend. A decimal is just a friendly way of writing a fraction when the whole is cut into ten or one hundred equal parts. Think of money: the tenths are your dimes and the hundredths are your pennies. When you're not sure which decimal is bigger, turn them both into hundredths and count!

lesson.answer: A decimal is a fraction of a whole cut into 10 or 100 equal parts — 0.25 means 25 hundredths, just like 25 cents out of one dollar.

practice.question: At the grocery store in Victoria, a granola bar costs $1.65. Write the cents part as a fraction in hundredths. Then, for your science project you cut two strings: one is 0.6 metres and the other is 0.55 metres. Which string is longer, and by how many hundredths of a metre?
practice.answer: The cents part is 65 hundredths of a dollar, which is 65 over 100 (that's $0.65). The 0.6 metre string is longer, because 0.6 is the same as 0.60, which is 60 hundredths, and 60 is more than 55. It is longer by 5 hundredths of a metre, which is 5 centimetres.
